description: Small concept-curriculum pilot for teaching the material affordance of squeezing.
notes: This pilot is general affordance teaching, not benchmark item generation.
The squeezed object or material should be central; hands, fingers, clamps, and surfaces should be pressure sources.
Start with 20 documents so generated quality can be inspected before scaling.
Squeeze should teach inward pressure plus material response: compression, denting, bulging, wrinkling, rebound, collapse, or contents release.
Boundary cases matter: rigid but grippable objects can be squeezed as a grip, but their material barely compresses.

concept_profile.definition: To apply inward pressure to a bounded object or material so it compresses, dents, bulges, wrinkles, releases contents, rebounds, or resists the force.
concept_profile.centrality_rule: The squeezed object or material must be the central participant; the document should not mainly teach about the hand, fingers, clamp, or person.
generation_guidance: Make the target object or material the thing being squeezed or failing to squeeze.
Name a pressure source when natural, such as a hand, fingers, palm, clamp, or two surfaces.
Describe the material response: compresses, dents, bulges, wrinkles, releases liquid, rebounds, crumples, compacts, or stays rigid.
Do not treat unbounded liquid or gas as directly squeezeable; only a container holding it can be squeezed.
For rigid but grippable objects, distinguish squeezing as a tight grip from actual material compression.
For granular materials in flexible bags, keep the bag/container and the shifting grains conceptually separate.

positive_subtypes.label: porous absorbent materials
positive_subtypes.mechanism: porous materials compress under pressure and may release stored water or air

positive_subtypes.label: filled flexible containers
positive_subtypes.mechanism: a flexible container changes shape and can force contents through an opening

positive_subtypes.label: juicy biological materials
positive_subtypes.mechanism: soft tissue compresses and may release juice from inside the material

positive_subtypes.label: soft cohesive deformable materials
positive_subtypes.mechanism: soft cohesive materials dent, flatten, bulge, or keep a new shape

positive_subtypes.label: elastic rebounding objects
positive_subtypes.mechanism: elastic objects compress under pressure and tend to rebound when released

positive_subtypes.label: fabrics and flexible sheets
positive_subtypes.mechanism: flexible sheets bunch, wrinkle, fold, and may release water if wet

positive_subtypes.label: granular materials in flexible bags
positive_subtypes.mechanism: the flexible bag deforms while the grains inside shift, pack, and redistribute

positive_subtypes.label: crumplable thin solids
positive_subtypes.mechanism: thin solids crease, buckle, or collapse rather than smoothly compressing

positive_subtypes.label: soft packed masses
positive_subtypes.mechanism: packed masses compact, crumble, hold together, or release moisture depending on structure

negative_subtypes.label: rigid but grippable boundary objects
negative_subtypes.reason: a hand can squeeze or grip the object, but the rigid material barely compresses

negative_subtypes.label: unbounded liquids
negative_subtypes.reason: unbounded liquid flows away; a person squeezes a container or soaked material, not the loose liquid itself

negative_subtypes.label: gases and vapors
negative_subtypes.reason: gas fills space and is not squeezed directly unless it is inside a bounded container

negative_subtypes.label: loose granular materials
negative_subtypes.reason: loose grains pour, scatter, or pile; they become squeezeable mainly when held in a flexible bag or packed mass

negative_subtypes.label: brittle or fixed rigid solids
negative_subtypes.reason: brittle or fixed rigid solids tend to crack, resist, or stay in place rather than compressing smoothly

state_contrasts.lesson: soft clay can be squeezed into a new shape; fired clay is rigid and may crack instead
soft dough dents and stretches when squeezed; baked bread crushes or tears rather than reshaping like dough
a wet sponge can be squeezed to release water; a dry stiff sponge compresses less and releases no liquid
a full sauce packet can be squeezed to push sauce out; an empty packet only crumples flat
a ripe orange can be squeezed for juice; dried peel bends or cracks with little juice to release

neighbors.label: press
neighbors.relation: nearby force action: pressing can be one-sided against a surface, while squeezing applies inward pressure around or into something

neighbors.label: pinch
neighbors.relation: nearby force action: pinching is narrow and usually uses fingertips, while squeezing can use more of the hand

neighbors.label: crush
neighbors.relation: nearby force outcome: crushing damages or collapses something more completely than ordinary squeezing

neighbors.label: wring
neighbors.relation: nearby action: wringing twists while squeezing, often to remove liquid from cloth

neighbors.label: grip
neighbors.relation: nearby hand action: gripping holds an object, while squeezing adds pressure that may deform it

neighbors.label: knead
neighbors.relation: nearby dough action: kneading repeatedly presses and folds, while squeezing compresses inward

neighbors.label: pour
neighbors.relation: contrast action: pouring transfers loose or flowing material instead of compressing a bounded object

neighbors.label: tap
neighbors.relation: contrast action: tapping is brief light contact, while squeezing sustains inward pressure

discourse_styles.description: A plain connective paragraph that places the target concept among nearby material behaviors.
guidance: Connect squeezing to a larger family of force and material-response behaviors instead of giving only one isolated example.
Name 2-3 nearby actions when natural, such as press, pinch, crush, wring, grip, knead, pour, or tap.
Explain why the target material fits squeezing and why at least one nearby behavior has a different boundary.

discourse_styles.description: Brief, concrete observations of what happens before, during, or after an everyday material event.
guidance: Use plain observed changes instead of abstract labels.
Keep the material behavior visible: compressing, denting, bulging, wrinkling, releasing liquid, rebounding, crumpling, compacting, cracking, or staying rigid.

discourse_styles.description: Simple explanatory prose with child-friendly vocabulary and visible causes.
guidance: Use short, clear causal language.
Avoid dense terminology and microscopic mechanisms.

discourse_styles.description: A small ordinary scene where a person uses, prepares, notices, or changes a material.
guidance: Make the scene ordinary and concrete.
Keep the squeezed material central rather than the person, hand, or tool.

discourse_styles.description: A compact explanation of the pressure source and the material's visible response.
guidance: Name the pressure source when natural, such as fingers, a hand, a palm, a clamp, or two surfaces.
Describe the response: compress, dent, bulge, wrinkle, release liquid, rebound, crumple, compact, crack, or resist.
Keep the lesson centered on the material response, not on the person applying force.

discourse_styles.description: A practical note about how to move, prepare, clean up, or handle a material under pressure.
guidance: Use a practical situation such as cleaning a sponge, using a tube, handling fruit, packing a bag, shaping clay, or testing whether something compresses.
Mention a nearby alternative action when the material does not squeeze cleanly, such as press, grip, scoop, pour, place, wipe, or let settle.
Keep the prose natural for pretraining, not a recipe checklist.

signal_orders.description: Start with the target affordance, then contrast with a negative or neighbor-winning case.
guidance: Lead with the material that fits the target action.
Then name a material, state, or neighbor action where the target action is not the best description.
Make the contrast explicit without turning the document into a quiz.

signal_orders.description: Start with the negative or neighbor-winning case, then explain the positive target affordance.
guidance: Lead with a material or state where the target action does not fit.
Then introduce the material that does fit the target action.
Use this order to reduce target-word-first bias.

signal_orders.description: Start by naming a nearby action that wins for another material, then contrast with the target action.
guidance: Begin with the neighbor action as the better description for one material.
Then explain why the target action fits the specified target material.
Keep both actions grounded in material behavior.

signal_orders.description: Start with the target action, then name the neighbor action that wins elsewhere.
guidance: Begin with the target action and the specified positive material.
Then name a neighbor action that is better for a different material or state.
Avoid implying the target action is the default for all materials.

signal_orders.description: Present two materials in parallel and assign different actions to each.
guidance: Use a parallel comparison of two materials or states.
Assign the target action to the material that supports it.
Assign a different neighbor action or response to the material that does not support it.
